vignette:
He is seventy-seven now, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life in operating rooms, where blood, urgency, and the edge between life and death are ordinary. For decades he has been known as a steady surgeon, the one whose hands do not shake, whose voice stays level even when everyone else in the room is tense. His wife says that before the event he carried the hospital home with him only in stories-small details over dinner, never the fear, never the faces. He believed in composure, in usefulness, in doing what had to be done and then moving on.

The moment that divides his life happens late one evening at the hospital. He is walking from one wing to another after finishing a long case when he hears shouting near the emergency entrance. At first he assumes it is the usual confusion of a busy night, but then he sees a young man collapse after being violently assaulted just outside the doors. There is too much blood, too much noise, too many people frozen for one terrible second before moving all at once. He runs toward the scene with two nurses. He kneels on the pavement in his scrubs and tries to help, pressing his hands where he knows to press, calling for equipment that is not there yet, hearing the man's choking breaths and then the sudden absence of them. What remains with him later is not only the sight of the injuries but the young man's eyes fixing on him as if asking for something he cannot give. Even after the emergency team takes over, he stands there feeling as though the world has split open in a place he had always considered safe.

That night he returns home long after midnight. His wife opens the door and immediately notices that he does not remove his shoes, does not speak, only goes to wash his hands again and again. He tells her there was "an incident," but the words sound thin and formal, as though he is presenting at rounds. He lies down but does not sleep. Each time he closes his eyes he sees the pavement under the fluorescent lights, hears the raw panic in the voices around him, feels the warmth of blood on his hands. By morning he has decided he must carry on. He goes back to the hospital because that is what he has always done.

In the weeks that follow, he expects the images to fade. Instead they sharpen. Certain sounds-a metal trolley rattling quickly down a hallway, someone shouting from a distance, ambulance sirens approaching the entrance-make his chest clench before he can think. He starts taking a different route through the hospital to avoid the emergency doors. If a case runs late and he has to cross that area at night, he feels his breathing turn shallow and his skin go cold. He tells himself he is being foolish. He is a surgeon; he has seen worse. That thought does not help. What troubles him most is that this event was not inside the contained order of the operating theatre. It was chaos, helplessness, exposure. He was there, he acted, and still the young man died.

At home he becomes restless and distant. His wife notices he startles when she comes up behind him in the kitchen. He begins checking the locks repeatedly before bed, then looking out the window if he hears voices on the street. Sleep comes in broken fragments. He wakes from dreams in which he is running toward someone he cannot reach, or in which he is back on the pavement with hands that will not move. On those nights he sits in the dark living room until dawn, unwilling to return to bed because he does not want to bring the dream back with him. During the day he grows irritable over small things-misplaced glasses, traffic, a question asked twice. He dislikes this in himself, especially with his grandchildren, who only know that Grandfather has become quieter and easier to unsettle.

At work he remains competent, but effort now goes into appearing unchanged. Before operations he washes his hands longer than necessary, lost for a moment in the memory of trying to scrub away blood that was not his patient's. He finds himself watching younger staff closely near moments of crisis, as if disaster is always about to break through the usual routine. Sometimes, in the middle of dictating notes, an image of the young man's face enters his mind so vividly that he loses his place. He has begun declining invitations to hospital gatherings held in the evening because they require passing the entrance where it happened. He says he is tired, which is true, though not in the simple way people mean.

He speaks about the event reluctantly over several sessions, with long pauses and an apologetic smile, as if he is embarrassed by the persistence of it. He says he has spent a lifetime teaching residents how to stay calm in catastrophe, yet now he feels ambushed by his own memory. He does not think of himself as afraid, exactly. He thinks of himself as altered. The world seems less orderly than it once did. Safety feels temporary. He still goes to the hospital, still operates, still sits each morning with tea his wife prepares, but he moves through his days with a sense that something violent can erupt without warning and leave him once again kneeling under harsh lights, trying and failing to hold a life in place.
